articles.title: A Michigan collector paid $30 for a painting overlooked at an estate sale; the 1951 work had vanished from public view for 75 years and is now estimated to fetch as much as $250,000
articles.summary: US News: A Michigan collector paid just $30 for a painting at an estate sale, not knowing that the work had been out of public view for about 75 years. The 195.
articles.body: A Michigan collector paid just $30 for a painting at an estate sale, not knowing that the work had been out of public view for about 75 years. The 1951 painting by American Surrealist Gertrude Abercrombie has since been authenticated and is now estimated to sell for $150,000 to $250,000 at Freeman’s New York on October 1.The painting, Alderman Merriam’s Shells, was found earlier this year at an estate sale in Michigan, according to Art Net News. The collector, who usually searches for vinyl records and mid-century furniture, spotted the work in a dark hallway leading towards a garage. A signature reading “abercrombie ’51” caught the collector’s attention, leading to the $30 purchase.The discovery became more significant when the new owner visited the Milwaukee Art Museum’s exhibition Gertrude Abercrombie: The Whole World Is a Mystery. While looking through the exhibition catalogue, the collector found an archival photograph of the same painting. The photograph had appeared in a September 1952 Chicago Tribune review of Abercrombie’s exhibition at Newman Brown Gallery in Chicago.The owner then contacted Dr Susan Weininger, a leading scholar of Abercrombie, who authenticated the painting. The work was identified as Alderman Merriam’s Shells, painted in 1951. It will now be among the highlights of Freeman’s Post-War & Contemporary Art auction in New York.Painting remained hidden for 75 yearsThe painting had a documented history before it disappeared from public view. Abercrombie gave it to Dr John Reynolds of Kalamazoo, Michigan, in early 1952 in exchange for medical services. It remained with Reynolds for the rest of his life and later passed through his estate and family.Before disappearing from public view, the painting had been exhibited several times. Freeman’s said it appeared in six solo exhibitions during 1952 and 1953. These included exhibitions at Newman Brown Gallery and Steven Gross Studios in Chicago, Edwin Hewitt Gallery in New York, Bresler Gallery in Milwaukee, Contemporary Arts Gallery in Evanston and Illinois Design Center in Chicago.The painting shows nine seashells arranged across a slate-grey surface. Another conical shell hangs from a thread against a black wall, appearing to float above the other shells.The work is unusual in Abercrombie’s career because it was painted directly from real objects. Freeman’s said the shells belonged to Robert Merriam, an alderman from Chicago’s Hyde Park neighbourhood, where Abercrombie lived and worked.Shells gave clue to Abercrombie’s workThe painting also provides information about Abercrombie’s use of shells as a recurring subject. A small central nautilus shell in the painting has a hole and a crack. Freeman’s said these details are echoed in some of her later solitary shell paintings, which had long been thought to have been invented.The rediscovered painting suggests that at least some of those details came from direct observation and memory. Shells had a particular symbolic importance in Abercrombie’s work. Freeman’s described them as representing protection and confinement, while their spiral shape could also serve as a talisman of friendship that she gave to people close to her.Zack Wirsum, senior vice president and head of the Post-War and Contemporary Art department at Freeman’s, described the discovery as an important moment for the auction house.“Little did I know that one of those 'once in a while's would occur less than a month later,” Wirsum said. He was referring to a comment he had made to visitors on an exhibition tour, when he said Abercrombie paintings still occasionally surfaced at estate sales.“We could not be more thrilled to now steward this magnificent rediscovery to the next chapter of its fascinating story,” he said.From estate sale to auctionThe collector’s discovery also came at a time when interest in Abercrombie’s work has increased. Artnet News reported that the artist’s reputation and market have grown following gallery and museum exhibitions since 2018.Abercrombie was a Chicago-based artist who did not have gallery representation and instead sold her works directly to collectors or gave them to friends. That history helps explain why some of her paintings can still emerge from private collections, according to Artnet News.Her work was largely overlooked for decades. In 2018, Karma gallery exhibited Abercrombie, describing her as an important but under-considered figure in mid-century American Surrealism. Museum exhibitions followed, bringing renewed attention to her paintings.Artnet’s Price Database shows the change in her art market. In the year before the 2018 Karma exhibition, Abercrombie’s paintings generated less than $75,000 in total sales, with prices generally around $10,000. Since then, 80 of her paintings have sold for more than $100,000, while 83% of works exceeded their high estimates.In November last year, Message for Mercy (1950), which features a cat in a stark interior, became the first Abercrombie painting to sell for more than $1 million. It sold at Sotheby’s New York for more than three times its high estimate.Artnet reported that Abercrombie’s four most expensive works have all been sold since 2024, while her total annual sales have repeatedly exceeded $3.5 million.Freeman’s auction includes other major worksAlderman Merriam’s Shells is part of Freeman’s Post-War & Contemporary Art auction, scheduled for October 1 at its New York saleroom. The sale will include works from several collections and periods of post-war American art.The auction will also feature sculptures by British artist Henry Moore from the collection of the Brooklyn Museum. These works include Two Piece Reclining Figure #6 from 1964, estimated at $30,000 to $50,000, and Slow Form: Tortoise from 1962, estimated at $20,000 to $30,000.Two works by American artist Alice Neel will also be offered. Judge Medina from 1949 and Judge Medina – Trial Scene from 1951–52 are each estimated at $30,000 to $50,000. The drawings were connected to the Smith Act trial of Communist Party leaders in the late 1940s and early 1950s.Another section of the sale will feature works from the Rosenthal Collection of Newtown, Pennsylvania. The collection is linked to Louis H. In a Sunday morning post, Trump said he is updating the plans at the "strong request" of the US military and for "national security purposes".

The "top grade" military complex and arch will "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage", he said.

He did not provide details on construction plans or timing, and it's not clear if he needs further approval for the facility.

"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington DC is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch", without specifying what those cities are.

Construction on Trump's 250-foot arch, planned for a site across the Potomac River from Washington DC just outside the Arlington National Cemetery, was expected to begin this month.

A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure. It will stand 250-feet (76m) from its base to the top of the golden lady statue.

At that height, the structure would dwarf the 99-foot Lincoln Memorial nearby and be half as high as the Washington Monument.

The BBC has contacted the Department of Defence for more information on the updated plans.

Trump has pursued a number of construction projects during his second term to revamp the US capital, including a gilded makeover of the Oval Office, constructing a White House ballroom estimated to cost around $400m, paving over the White House Rose Garden, and renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The triumphal arch is one of the biggest projects Trump has set his sights on.

articles.title: Hamas allegedly built weapons depots across Europe, planned terror attacks as Oct 7 anniversary neared
articles.summary: Federal German prosecutors indicted seven suspects who allegedly stockpiled weapons for Hamas to target Jewish communities and Israeli diplomats.
articles.body: The German federal prosecutor’s office recently announced that it indicted seven people for allegedly securing weapons for the Hamas terrorist organization, with the goal of launching terrorist attacks on the second remembrance date of the Oct. 7 massacre in Israel. The indictment has catapulted the danger of Hamas’ network in Europe to Israeli, American and European installations and citizens into the spotlight. According to the prosecutor’s office, "All of the accused belong to the foreign terrorist organization Hamas. Some time ago, the organization’s military wing (the so-called Qassam Brigades) began establishing weapons depots in Europe. No later than July 2025, Hamas planned a concrete assassination in Germany or Austria targeting representatives of Israel, people of Jewish faith, or persons with pro-Israel views." The seven suspects were arrested between October 2025 and May 2026. SUSPECTED HAMAS TERRORIST ARRESTED IN GREECE FOR ALLEGEDLY PLOTTING ATTACK ON ISRAELI CRUISE SHIP The statement added, "The attack was to take place in close temporal proximity to the second anniversary of Hamas’s assault on Israel on 7 October 2023 — i.e., in early October 2025." The indictment listed the nationalities and first names and first letter of the last name of the suspects: German national Abed Al G., Danish national Yousif C., Lebanon-born Borhan El-K., Lebanon-born Wael F.M., German national Ahmad I., Lebanon-born Kamel M., Bulgarian national Mohammad S." German law shields the last names of criminal suspects for privacy reasons. The German prosecutors said the suspected Hamas terrorists "had already obtained a functional fully automatic rifle, 13 functional pistols and more than 700 rounds of ammunition. Mohammed A., who is being prosecuted separately, transported some of the weapons to Vienna and stored them there." According to the German paper Die Welt, "One of the accused was working as a confidential informant for Germany’s domestic intelligence agency. The files show that the informant continued reporting to his intelligence handler while allegedly failing to disclose the full extent of his own involvement in obtaining ammunition for the group." EXCLUSIVE: ISRAEL SEIZES VAST IRAN TERROR AXIS ARSENAL WITH SURPRISING FOREIGN ORIGINS Sascha Adamek, a German journalist and the author of the 2026 book "Infiltration: Political Islam Continues Its Advance," told Fox News Digital, "Now the policy of previous federal governments is coming back to haunt them: until 2023 they allowed Hamas and its front organizations to use Germany as a ‘safe haven’ for fundraising and recruitment and also for the radicalization of young people. This dirty deal — that Hamas does not use violence in this country and is therefore left to operate freely — has long been obsolete." According to the most recent Federal German domestic intelligence report, Hamas could have had as many as 650 operatives in Germany during 2025, the last year of tracking. In 2024, 550 Hamas operatives were active and in 2023 the number totaled 450. The intelligence officials wrote in the report that "The figures refer to Germany and are partly estimated and rounded." According to the report, 1,250 Hezbollah operatives are active in Germany. UN AGENCY ACCUSED OF HAMAS TIES SEES ANOTHER EUROPEAN NATION CUT FUNDING When asked why Germany is allowing Hamas and Hezbollah operatives and members to conduct activities within its territory, the press office of the German Federal Ministry of the Interior told Fox News Digital in part, "Hamas, which has been banned from operating in Germany since 2023, has a network of supporters and followers; however, for many years they have tended to act with restraint in public and avoid any outward signs of connection to the organization." The Interior Ministry’s press office added, "Hezbollah, which is also subject to a ban on its activities in Germany, is not organized under any nationwide umbrella organization or similar supraregional structure. Rather, its supporters are spread across various associations throughout Germany. The focus of the activities of these associations — which are classified as affiliated with Hezbollah —lies in the religious and cultural spheres, as well as in educational programs for children, youth and adults that promote conservative Islam and a Shi’ite identity. In isolated cases, Hezbollah supporters in Germany have been known to engage in specific acts of support for the organization in Lebanon." When asked if the German government is lax, as critics argue, about eradicating Hamas and Hezbollah terrorism structures, the Interior Ministry said, "On November 2, 2023, the Federal Ministry of the Interior banned the activities of the terrorist organization Hamas in Germany, as these activities violate German criminal law and run counter to the principle of international understanding… Furthermore, its purpose or activities significantly harm the interests of the Federal Republic of Germany. In addition, the Federal Ministry of the Interior had already banned the activities of Hezbollah in Germany on April 30, 2020, as these activities also violate German criminal law and the organization is directed against the principle of international understanding." The interior ministry noted, "Federal and state security authorities consistently investigate leads regarding possible extremist activities as well as acts subject to criminal prosecution and continuously examine all countermeasures available under the rule of law." The statement also said, "The Hamas terrorist attack on the State of Israel on October 7, 2023, and the subsequent military operation by Israeli defense forces in the Gaza Strip continue to have an impact on the security situation in Germany and Europe. In addition to the heightened abstract threat level, there continue to be intense pro-Palestinian protests as well as corresponding agitation on social media. Various extremist actors in Germany are inciting hatred and violence against Jews or the State of Israel, or denying its right to exist." GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS The presence of indicted Lebanese men highlights the alliance between the two U.S-designated terrorist organizations, Hamas and the Lebanon-based Hezbollah. The Iranian regime-backed Hezbollah joined Hamas a day after the Gaza-based terrorist movement invaded Israel in 2023 and slaughtered over 1,200 people. Germany's Die Welt reported, "The prosecutors alleged the weapons operation was also coordinated from Lebanon, where a Hamas operative allegedly oversaw one of the procurement channels linking members of the network across Europe." Israel’s Foreign Ministry seized on the report about the planned Hamas terror attacks in Germany and Austria, posting on X: "Palestinian Hamas was planning terror on the streets of Europe. German prosecutors say Hamas plotted attacks in Berlin and Vienna targeting Jewish communities and Israeli diplomats – part of a network allegedly using Turkey as a base for terror operations against European targets. The goal: mark October 7 with more blood." Matthew Levitt, a leading scholar on Hezbollah and Hamas in Europe from the Washington Institute, told Fox News Digital, "I wrote the only long form, detailed expose on this a while back now in CTC Sentinel [Combating Terrorism Center}, based on court documents and extensive interviews." He added, "Hamas continues plotting in Europe, overseen by senior Qassam Brigades officials in Lebanon and with direct ties to senior Hamas leadership. One of the people arrested in Europe is the son of a senior Hamas leader, Basem Naim." Levitt published his article titled "Hamas Plots in Europe: A Shift Toward External Operations?" in the October 2025 issue of the West Point journal CTC. Levitt cited a 2024 German prosecution indictment of alleged Hezbollah terrorists planning possible attacks against an American military base and Israel's embassy. Levitt wrote, "The weapons, German officials concluded, ‘were intended to expand Hamas’ activities in Europe.‘ As the investigation progressed, German authorities determined — based on materials found on one of the defendants’ USB storage devices — that the Hamas operatives were considering specific targets in Germany, including the Israeli embassy in Berlin, the U.S. Ramstein Air Base in Rhineland-Palatinate and the area around Berlin’s Tempelhof airport." articles.title: The pro-Israel censors are starting to lose
articles.summary: The Macklemore controversy demonstrates that the cost of speaking up for Palestine is diminishing.
articles.body:
For decades, Israel’s greatest advantage in the West was not simply military or political support. It was narrative power.

Israel and its supporters enjoyed enormous influence over the boundaries of acceptable discussion about Palestine: which violent incident received attention, whose security mattered the most, which historical context was relevant and, crucially, what criticism of Israel could be allowed in public.

That power has not disappeared. But the extraordinary controversy surrounding Macklemore’s removal from Ed Sheeran’s US tour shows how rapidly it is eroding.

The fact that the American rapper was dropped from the tour after he spoke about Palestine on stage meant that the old system worked. A powerful billionaire objected. Venues applied pressure. The artist disappeared from the stage.

What was different this time was the backlash.

In response to the censorship, every remaining support act on Sheeran’s tour walked away. Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Beoga all withdrew. Meanwhile, ticket prices for Sheeran’s remaining concerts plunged, in some cases losing 50 percent of their value, as many fans felt outraged.

Macklemore stood his ground and pledged the $1m he had earned from his appearances to six organisations supporting Palestinians. Subsequently, the media reported Sheeran would donate $2m towards humanitarian relief in the region.

All of this has helped generate further donations and attention for Palestinian aid organisations, including a $1m pledge from children’s educator Ms Rachel.

An attempt to push “Free Palestine” off the stage resulted in Palestine receiving vastly more attention, artists abandoning one of the world’s biggest tours and more funds being donated to Palestinian organisations.

The attempt to control the message amplified the message itself. And that tells us something much bigger than how controversy is handled in the music industry.

Amid its genocide in Gaza, Israel is facing a crisis not simply of public opinion, but of narrative control.

For almost three years, the world has watched Palestinians killed, displaced and starved. It has seen neighbourhoods flattened, hospitals overwhelmed and families repeatedly driven from one place to another. A United Nations Commission of Inquiry has concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.

The old narrative increasingly struggles against a force Israel cannot easily control: people can see what is happening themselves.

Palestinian journalists, doctors, parents and ordinary citizens no longer depend entirely on Western governments or established media organisations to narrate their lives. Images, testimony and documentation travel directly from Gaza to millions of phones around the world.

There are limits to propaganda when people can witness the consequences of power for themselves. Public opinion increasingly reflects that rupture.

A Pew Research Center survey across 36 countries this year found a median of 67 percent of respondents held an unfavourable view of Israel. In the United Kingdom, it was 69 percent, Germany – 73 percent, Italy – 75 percent and Australia – 79 percent. Even in the United States, Israel’s most important ally, 60 percent viewed Israel unfavourably.

Among younger people, the transformation is more dramatic still. Seventy-four percent of Americans aged 18 to 34 surveyed by Pew viewed Israel unfavourably, as did 78 percent of young Britons and 87 percent of young Australians.

This does not mean everyone supports Palestine or agrees on what a political settlement should look like. It means that the cost of speaking up for Palestine is falling.

For years, the implied question confronting artists, academics and other public figures openly supporting Palestine was: what are you prepared to lose? Your booking? Your sponsorship? Your reputation? Your career?

The purpose of such consequences was larger than the individual. Punish one person publicly and hundreds of others would understand the warning and keep silent.

But deterrence only works when people are deterred.

This time, they weren’t. And that put pressure on the censors and those who complied.

The backlash forced Sheeran to speak up publicly about Palestine. On Saturday, during his concert in Philadelphia, where he had to play solo, he called what is happening in Gaza “unjustifiable”.

Speaking for Palestine can still carry a professional cost. Macklemore has just demonstrated that. But increasingly, censors may discover that silencing pro-Palestine voices carries a cost, too.

That is why the Israeli narrative crisis runs deeper than falling approval ratings.

The old power was not merely the ability to silence Palestinians and those who stood with them. It was the ability to determine which account of Palestine the world would hear. That monopoly is breaking.

They succeeded in removing the man who said “Free Palestine” from the stage. But “Free Palestine” became louder.

And that may be the clearest indication yet that Israel is not simply losing an argument. It is losing its grip on the story.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Exhibition celebrates legacy of arts educator Sir Roy Shaw
articles.summary: Sir Roy Shaw served as the Secretary-General of the Arts Council and was knighted in 1979.
articles.body:
The life of a professor and former Arts Council Secretary-General for England is being honoured in an exhibition, 14 years after his death.

Sir Roy Shaw, who served as Keele University's Director of Adult Education from 1962 to 1975, will be celebrated for his lifelong commitment to arts.

He was knighted in 1979 in recognition of his major contributions to adult education and helping shape national policies.

The exhibition, which opened on Saturday, will run at the Staffordshire university's Chancellor's building until 28 October.

The exhibition will bring together material from Sheffield-born Sir Roy's personal academic archive, alongside family photographs and artefacts.

Despite an impoverished upbringing he went on to play an important role in national arts and education policy and supported regional theatre through his work with Peter Cheeseman and the Victoria Theatre in Stoke-on-Trent.

Alongside the exhibition, visitors can discover the stories of other influential changemakers whose achievements have been recognised by Keele through the award of honorary degrees.

A public lecture will also taking place in Chancellor's Building on 5 October between 18:00 and 20:00 BST

articles.body: A single gunshot during a post-tailgate fight near Notre Dame's South Bend, Indiana campus struck a woman and a police officer Saturday night, authorities said. POLICE MAKE ARREST AFTER GUNFIRE DURING CALIFORNIA HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL GAME LEAVES 1 DEAD Both victims were transported to a local hospital and are expected to make full recoveries. Police said the officer was "doing fine," and that the woman was "okay." Notre Dame officials said the suspected shooter fled west from the scene, NBC 5 Chicago reported. The suspect reportedly remains at large. and was described as a heavyset Black male with dreadlocks, wearing blue shorts, a black shirt with a red and blue design on the front, and missing one shoe, according to the local report. MULTIPLE PEOPLE KILLED IN SHOOTING AT IDAHO IN-N-OUT RESTAURANT, SUSPECT DEAD Following the incident, police swiftly evacuated nearby businesses and parking garages. The South Bend Police Department locked down the busy commercial district for an active investigation, urging the public to avoid the area while a heavy police presence secured the scene. articles.title: Justice minister 'deeply concerned' over temporary release of convicted killer
articles.summary: Gary Anderson was released on Monday from Maghaberry Prison to attend the funeral of his father but absconded and remains at large.
articles.body:
The justice minister remains "deeply concerned" about the circumstances surrounding the temporary release of a convicted murderer.

The NI Prison Service (NIPS) refused Gary Anderson permission to attend his father's funeral but that decision was quashed by the courts.

Anderson was released on Monday from Maghaberry Prison to attend the funeral but absconded and remains at large.

He is one of two brothers jailed for life in 2023 for the 2018 murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry.

The court service has now published the full 15 page judgement from the judicial review. It reveals the decision to refuse Anderson's request to attend the funeral was taken by the duty governor at Maghaberry Prison.

But the judge found that that decision "was based upon inaccurate information which was material to the key issue of the potential risks posed by the applicant".

"The information which was considered was also materially disadvantageous to the applicant."

That's a reference to an internal assessment of the likelihood of Anderson reoffending, which was wrongly recorded at a higher level than recorded in the internal system.

A legal representative for the prison service admitted to the court that "information containing an increased score came, not from the duty governor's personal knowledge, but from a colleague. When the system was checked, the score was sitting at 27 (medium likelihood) and not 32 (high likelihood) as stated in the decision letter."

The judge, Mr Justice Rooney, found "the duty governor clearly took account of this incorrect information when making his own risk assessment and when conducting a proportionality assessment".

He invited the duty governor to review the decision but that offer was declined, in a move the judge described as "somewhat surprising".

In a statement, the Justice department said that "this opportunity was not communicated by legal representatives to those within NIPS who held responsibility for the decision".

"Updates provided to NIPS following the hearing, including legal readouts, did not indicate such an opportunity had been offered."

Mr Justice Rooney granted Anderson temporary release with a number of conditions attached after finding that the prison service's decision was "flawed" and took into account "irrelevant and incorrect factors". He added "the failure to secure and take account of the correct risk assessment is unlawful".

The department said Minister Naomi Long "remains deeply concerned surrounding compassionate temporary release of Gary Anderson and his subsequent absconding".

Following a review of the case, further information emerged regarding the handling of the case.

"As soon as the minister was made aware of these issues, she instructed the director general of the Northern Ireland Prison Service to undertake an urgent investigation into these matters."

"The minister is clear that it is important that all relevant facts are established and considered carefully, and she intends to update the assembly at the earliest opportunity as to the actions she will be taking to ensure that this happens."

'Catastrophic and inexplicable failures'

Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader, Jon Burrows described the judgement as "damning" adding "it exposes catastrophic and inexplicable failures in senior decision-making, procedure and record-keeping at Maghaberry Prison".

"The substantive decision to refuse Gary Anderson compassionate temporary release was, in my view, clearly correct. His subsequent absconding has only underlined the serious risk he presented.

"However, that decision was catastrophically undermined by incorrect information, missing records and an extraordinary refusal to reconsider it when the court provided an opportunity to do so.

"This was not a minor administrative error. The incorrect information went directly to the assessment of the risk posed by a convicted murderer and was expressly relied upon in refusing his release.

"The decision collapsed because it relied upon materially incorrect information, the assessment supposedly supporting it could not be produced and the duty governor refused the opportunity to reconsider.

"The family of Karol Kelly and the wider public deserve the full truth, urgent accountability and firm action to ensure that this can never happen again."

articles.title: The 48-hour city: Why people are investing in second homes in Vrindavan
articles.summary: News News: There has been a quiet but definite transformation taking place in the residential real estate of India regarding the meaning of a house. A house is n.
articles.body: There has been a quiet but definite transformation taking place in the residential real estate of India regarding the meaning of a house. A house is no longer confined only to the city where the urban dweller works and spends his weekdays. Weekend living and the need for houses that offer a confluence of connectivity, comfort, spirituality and leisure have led to the birth of such a trend. Vrindavan is proving to be one of the favored destinations among others for this phenomenon.The concept of ‘48-hour city’ represents a new trend in home buying. While the buyers continue to live in their current city like Delhi-NCR and other big cities during the week, they now have a home away from their current city to spend their weekends, extended weekends, holidays and family vacation time. Ankit Aggarwal, Director, Devika Group shares insightson how Vridavan is evolving into a second home investment place for people living around Delhi/NCR.A place for the soulVrindavan has been a draw in the past due to its significance in terms of spirituality and culture. But now, the kind of visitor is beginning to change. The family visitor is opting for long-term stay over temple-visits. This means that quality accommodation and residences which offer more privacy and comfort have become a necessity. Thus, this will mean that the profile of the property buyer is also widening. There will not only be those who are buying a permanent home but there will also be people who wish to buy a holiday home in a place such as this.The buyer is interested in being closer to places of spiritual significance, but he/she is also interested in other aspects of the community.Connectivity is altering the equationThe demand for weekend homes largely revolves around accessibility. As the destination becomes more easily accessible, it makes it easier and more economical for urban dwellers to invest in and make use of their second home. In the case of buyers from the Delhi-NCR region, the overall growth of the Mathura-Vrindavan area makes the prospects of shorter durations much more attractive. Better connectivity and other infrastructural facilities may make it easier to plan trips to the area.This is crucial because second homes need to be used in order to generate value. A weekend getaway that is easy to access over two days is very different from one that requires elaborate planning in terms of connectivity.What is important for today’s weekend home buyerThe new age second home buyer is also becoming more choosy. The new buyer takes into consideration not just the size of apartments and the cost involved but the entire living experience. Properly designed open spaces, landscaping, community facilities, health facilities, security, and proper maintenance facilities can have a strong effect on the buying decision. The houses which are easy to maintain and stay comfortable even if not used on a regular basis are highly relevant for weekend use. Thus, the developers have the option of developing residential communities around weekend and extended use.A home that is emotionally and financially valuableApart from the practicalities of investment, a Vrindavan property might have some sentimental significance as well, related to spiritual values, family traditions, and the preferred lifestyle of the buyer. However, at the same time, the buyers should consider these purchases as rational decisions. articles.title: Israeli man shot dead near West Bank settlement, Netanyahu orders demolition of ‘terrorist’ home
articles.summary: Middle East News: An Israeli man in his 30s was shot dead near the West Bank settlement of Neve Tzuf, also known as Halamish, on Sunday, hours before the start of the Y.
articles.body: An Israeli man in his 30s was shot dead near the West Bank settlement of Neve Tzuf, also known as Halamish, on Sunday, hours before the start of the Yom Kippur holiday. The suspected attacker, who was injured while fleeing the scene, was later arrested at a hospital, according to the Israeli military.The victim was identified as Netanel Shukrun, a father of six who lived in the West Bank settlement of Alei Zahav, The Times of Israel reported. Shukrun had gone to a natural spring near Neve Tzuf with his eldest son to immerse in the water ahead of Yom Kippur, when the shooting took place.How the attack unfoldedAccording to the Israel Defense Forces, the suspected attacker opened fire toward the spring from a vehicle before getting out and fleeing on foot while still armed. Shukrun was seriously wounded and taken to Beilinson Hospital in Petah Tikva, where he later died.Footage shared on social media showed people at the spring ducking for cover as gunshots were heard in the area.The military said a combat tracker from the Binyamin Regional Brigade opened fire at the attacker as he fled, injuring him. The suspect then returned to his vehicle and drove to a hospital near Ramallah, where Israeli commandos from the Duvdevan Unit later arrested him based on information from the Shin Bet.The suspect's vehicle parked outside the hospital was also seized, the IDF said.Separately, the military said soldiers shot dead a Palestinian man who allegedly attempted to ram troops with his vehicle near the site of the former settlement of Ganim in the northern West Bank. Another Palestinian who was in the vehicle was detained, while no Israeli soldiers were injured, according to the IDF.What Netanyahu saidIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the attacks and said that "no terrorist is immune, nor are those who assisted them."Netanyahu said he had instructed Israeli security forces to send reinforcements to the West Bank, impose closures and carry out arrests.“We will hold them all accountable — in Gaza, in Lebanon, and in Judea and Samaria,” he said in a statement.He also ordered the immediate demolition of the home of "the terrorist", though it was unclear which of the two attackers he was referring to."On behalf of all the citizens of Israel, my wife and I send our deepest condolences to the family of the victim of the attack and share in their profound grief," Netanyahu said.Shukrun worked as a systems information analyst, while his wife Meirav is a lecturer at Ariel University, according to The Times of Israel. Samaria Regional Council head Yossi Dagan described him as a "man of kindness" and "humble and a lover of people."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Electric Mercedes motorhome targets 621-mile range
articles.summary: The Mercedes-Benz eActros 600 electric truck targets 621 miles per charge on a 28,000-mile round-the-world journey through over 30 countries.
articles.body: If you think you've seen some wild RVs, this one may reset the scale. Professional truck driver and content creator Tobias Wagner, better known online as Elektrotrucker, is preparing to drive around the world in a specially converted Mercedes-Benz eActros 600. A full Bliss Mobil living module sits behind the cab, turning this electric truck into a rolling home. Wagner plans to make the entire journey on battery power. Mercedes-Benz Trucks says the route will cover about 28,000 miles through more than 30 countries over roughly one year, with a goal of no more than 80 charging stops. According to Mercedes, the trip would be the first known circumnavigation of the globe in a fully battery-electric truck. What really caught my attention is how far Wagner hopes to go between those stops. Here's how this massive electric motorhome works and why its 621-mile range target could be the toughest part of the trip. 100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com This electric Mercedes motorhome started as a long-haul truck Underneath the living quarters sits the Mercedes-Benz eActros 600, a battery-electric truck built for long-distance commercial freight. Its three lithium iron phosphate battery packs provide a combined installed capacity of 621 kWh. Mercedes normally designs the truck to travel about 310 miles under specific fully loaded long-haul test conditions. Wagner's expedition truck has a very different job. Instead of pulling a heavily loaded commercial trailer, it carries a custom living module. Mercedes also modified the truck with single rear tires and expedition equipment. Those changes help reduce weight and rolling resistance compared with a traditional freight configuration. The finished expedition vehicle reportedly has a maximum weight of about 34,170 pounds. Power comes from Mercedes' electric axle and four-speed transmission. The eActros 600 produces about 536 horsepower continuously, with peak output reaching roughly 805 horsepower. That's a lot of muscle for a vehicle carrying its own kitchen and bed. Could it really travel 621 miles on one charge? This is where the project gets especially interesting. Wagner and Mercedes believe the lighter expedition setup, combined with careful hypermiling, could potentially travel as far as 621 miles on a single charge. That would be roughly double the range Mercedes quotes for a fully loaded eActros 600. Mercedes says the lighter expedition vehicle should significantly exceed the eActros 600's normal long-haul range. How close he gets will depend on road conditions, temperature, speed and terrain. Why the 621-mile target could become important Wagner wants to travel about 28,000 miles while stopping to charge no more than 80 times. That works out to an average of roughly 350 miles of driving per charging stop, although the actual distances will vary considerably along the route. Some stretches could become much more challenging. The expedition will cross regions where high-powered truck charging remains difficult to find. The latest route includes Central and East Asia, Australia, the United States and several countries in Latin America. That's where stretching the truck well beyond its normal freight range could become useful. ROBOTAXI PIT STOPS COULD POP UP NEAR YOU Charging a 621-kWh battery takes serious power Eventually, even this giant battery has to plug in. The eActros 600 supports CCS2 fast charging at up to 400 kW. Mercedes says that level of charging can take the battery from 10% to 80% in about 70 minutes under its specified conditions. Mercedes has also demonstrated Megawatt Charging System technology at up to 1,000 kW, which can cut charging times dramatically on compatible equipment. Wagner's expedition setup has also been prepared for different charging systems around the world. It includes charging connections positioned on both sides of the truck. The project also has adapters designed for charging infrastructure in China and North America. That flexibility could prove essential once the truck leaves Europe. Mercedes revealed another important backup. Wagner has equipped the truck with his own Alpitronic DC charging station. That lets him charge from AC connections at up to 43 kW in special situations when conventional high-powered truck charging is not available. The back of the truck is a fully electric home Bliss Mobil added a roughly 13-foot expedition module behind the cab. Inside, Wagner gets a U-shaped dining area along with a kitchen. A bathroom sits toward the rear. There's also a drop-down bed that stores above the dining area when he wants more room during the day. The camper can sleep as many as four people. Wagner will have considerably more room because his primary travel companion is his dog, Krümelix. The living module also follows the electric theme. It uses a separate 400-Ah lithium battery supported by 1,000 watts of solar power. That system handles equipment such as the induction cooktop, refrigerator and air conditioning. It also powers other onboard systems without relying on diesel or propane. The motorhome reportedly carries about 106 gallons of fresh water. A multistage filtration system helps Wagner manage water during extended stretches away from traditional campgrounds. The camper can operate separately from the truck Bliss Mobil designed the expedition module as a largely self-contained unit. Its electrical and plumbing systems sit within the camper rather than depending on the truck itself. That approach allows Bliss Mobil modules to move between compatible truck chassis. Wagner's module does have a 24-volt connection to the eActros. That means the living area can draw energy from the truck's main battery when necessary. Still, the expedition has an obvious reason to conserve that electricity. Every bit of power used inside the camper could otherwise help move a nearly 17-ton vehicle farther down the road. There's an electric motorcycle riding on the back A giant expedition truck can handle plenty of roads, but there will always be places where its size becomes a problem. Wagner has another electric solution for that. A motorcycle carrier on the back holds a Honda WN7 electric motorcycle. When the road becomes too tight for the eActros, Wagner can leave the motorhome behind and continue on two wheels. The motorcycle uses a 9.3-kWh battery and produces about 67 horsepower. It's a useful backup for a trip designed to reach places far beyond normal highway rest stops. TOYOTA JOINS HYDROGEN TRUCK ALLIANCE PUSH Nearly $800,000 buys one very unusual motorhome None of this comes cheaply. A price sheet displayed with the vehicle broke down the cost of the eActros 600 truck, Bliss Mobil camper and additional equipment. The total is approximately $796,600 including tax based on the exchange rate used at the time. Call it nearly $800,000. The Honda electric motorcycle wasn't included in that figure. Of course, this also isn't a production RV you can configure at your local Mercedes dealership. Wagner's vehicle is a specialized one-off expedition build created around a commercial electric truck. We've seen other companies rethink how electric vehicles fit into camping. The CyberTrailer takes a different approach, using solar power and an onboard energy system to support off-grid travel. The around-the-world trip starts Sept. 20 Mercedes-Benz Trucks says Wagner will officially depart from IAA Transportation 2026 in Hanover, Germany, on Sunday, Sept. 20. From there, the trip is expected to last about a year. Mercedes says Wagner will travel through around 30 countries on five continents while putting battery-electric truck technology through real-world conditions well beyond familiar European freight routes. Mercedes says the planned route may still change as the trip progresses. The vehicle may be built for an extraordinary adventure, but the results could tell us something much bigger about electric transportation. What this means to you You probably won't be putting an $800,000 electric expedition truck in your driveway. Still, this trip could answer questions that eventually affect far more ordinary electric vehicles. Range is only part of the EV equation. Reliable charging becomes even more important when you leave major highways or travel through areas with limited infrastructure. Wagner will be testing both. If the eActros can consistently travel well beyond its standard commercial range, engineers will get another example of how vehicle weight and driving technique can change battery performance. The charging side may prove equally revealing. A vehicle can carry an enormous battery, but long-distance travel still depends on finding equipment powerful enough to recharge it. Wagner's onboard charging equipment gives him another option when high-powered public chargers are unavailable, but slower charging could add considerable time to the trip. We have already seen experiments that attack the charging problem from another direction. One electric road project is testing technology that can transfer power to vehicles while they drive. Wagner's trip takes the opposite approach. He is bringing a huge battery and finding out how far today's infrastructure can take it. Kurt's key takeaways I love a good road trip, but this one takes the idea to another level. What fascinates me most isn't simply whether Wagner can squeeze 621 miles out of this massive battery. I want to see what happens when he leaves the easy charging routes behind and has to make this technology work across more than 30 countries. That's where this trip could get really interesting. A giant battery and impressive range numbers are great, but you still need a working charger when you pull in. If Wagner can circle the globe with roughly 80 charging stops, that's a pretty strong demonstration of how far electric trucking has come. And if he gets stranded looking for power along the way, we'll learn something from that, too. articles.title: Waltz delivers blunt warning to nations defying Iran sanctions, touts Greenland deal
articles.summary: USUN Ambassador Mike Waltz says President Trump will push Gulf leaders and allies to enforce Iran sanctions at the United Nations, warning of consequences for noncompliance.
articles.body: UNITED NATIONS, NEW YORK: President Donald Trump will return to the United Nations this week seeking greater international cooperation in confronting Iran, even as his administration moves to reshape the global institution hosting world leaders, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview ahead of the gathering. US presses allies to enforce Iran sanctions ahead of the UN General Assembly With the U.S.-Iran war entering its seventh month, Trump is expected to address the General Assembly on Tuesday and meet Gulf leaders whose countries have been directly affected by the conflict. The gathering comes as Washington seeks to intensify economic pressure on Tehran, European allies confront Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine and the administration faces questions about whether its push to reduce the U.N.'s size and spending risks diminishing the organization's ability to respond to international crises. BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY Waltz outlined what Washington expects from its partners on Iran: full enforcement of sanctions against Tehran, with consequences for countries that fail to comply. "They will reinforce that message, but importantly, it's all of these countries actually enforcing the sanctions and what they're going to hear is there will be consequences for friend and foe," Waltz said. "The president is doing this for the future security of the world." European and Asian allies have largely resisted Trump's requests for assistance in the Iran conflict, which began with U.S. and Israeli strikes in February, Reuters reported on on Sept. 18. The war has also disrupted energy markets, with Iran obstructing shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and its Houthi allies tightening their grip on a critical Red Sea shipping corridor. Waltz said the administration intends to make sanctions enforcement a central part of its diplomatic push during UNGA. "The Iranian economy continues to crater," Waltz said, pointing to the country's currency, inflation and the U.S. naval blockade. "One way or another, the president has been crystal clear on our goals here that Iran cannot and will not have a nuclear weapon." His remarks follow a Sept. 17 U.N. Security Council vote in which Russia and China blocked an effort to continue independent monitoring of international sanctions on Iran. Trump is also expected to meet Gulf leaders to discuss the conflict and regional security. Waltz said that the administration wants to hear directly from its Gulf partners about their concerns, describing the collective meeting as an important diplomatic opportunity. JEFF BARTOS SAYS UN REFORM IS NO LONGER AN 'OXYMORON' AFTER $570M IN CUTS A UN the Trump administration wants to change — but not abandon The Iran conflict is unfolding against a broader debate over the future of the United Nations, an institution Trump has repeatedly criticized and his administration has sought to substantially reform. On Sept. 16, the United States paid $725 million toward the U.N.'s regular budget and another $102 million for peacekeeping operations. The payments reduced Washington's outstanding debt and averted the immediate risk of losing its General Assembly voting rights in 2027. However, the U.S. still owed approximately $1.312 billion to the organization's regular budget, according to the U.N. Asked why American taxpayers should continue funding an organization the administration has repeatedly criticized for what it considers anti-American bias, Waltz pointed to efforts to reduce spending and redirect the institution toward its original mission. "The president is clear about getting the U.N. back to basics and helping it realize its potential," Waltz told Fox News Digital. He said the administration had secured more than $1 billion in budget reductions, with roughly 3,000 headquarters positions being cut and a reduction of approximately 25% in peacekeeping personnel. "We have the U.N. on a diet," Waltz said. But Waltz also made clear that the administration does not intend to abandon the United Nations. "There's got to be one place in the world where everyone can come together and put diplomacy first and can actually talk," he said. "We don't ever want to see a U.N. in Beijing or Moscow or Brussels." "If we just walked away, you'd have 192 countries talking without us," Waltz added. Gaza offers one example of how the administration intends to use the U.N. while limiting direct American military involvement. Waltz pointed to the U.N.-endorsed Board of Peace and the planned International Stabilization Force, which is intended to support security and a postwar transition in Gaza. The ambassador said he does not want American troops deployed there, arguing that international security operations should allow other countries to share the burden. The U.N. Security Council endorsed the Gaza peace plan and authorized the stabilization force in November 2025. The State Department said Sept. 18 that Secretary of State Marco Rubio will be in New York from Sept. 20–23 to meet foreign counterparts, advance U.S. security and economic priorities and continue the administration's campaign for U.N. reform. WALTZ CALLS OUT IRANIAN DIPLOMAT AT UN FOLLOWING DRONE STRIKES ON BAHRAIN AND KUWAIT Greenland agreement adds another dimension to allied diplomacy Trump arrives in New York days after announcing a new security agreement with Denmark and Greenland aimed at expanding the American military presence in the Arctic while restricting adversaries from establishing bases or making sensitive investments on the island. The agreement falls short of Trump's earlier ambition to acquire Greenland, which remains an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Denmark and Greenland have stressed that the arrangement will not compromise the island's sovereignty or right to self-determination. Additional details of the agreement have yet to be made public. Waltz told Fox News Digital that the deal reflects the Arctic's growing strategic importance as melting ice opens new shipping routes and increases access to energy and mineral resources. "It's incredibly significant," Waltz said, pointing to Russia's Arctic military capabilities and the potential for new shipping routes to transform global trade. "It took some tough tweets, maybe some tough language," he said. "We now have an agreement with our ally Denmark." The agreement comes as European governments confront overlapping security challenges involving Russia's war in Ukraine, Arctic defense and uncertainty over transatlantic security arrangements, while Washington seeks greater allied cooperation in its campaign against Iran. TRUMP ARRIVES AT NATO SUMMIT AS IRAN RIFT LOOMS ABOVE ALLIANCE TALKS World leaders converge on New York The U.N. expects 73 heads of state and 45 heads of government, along with 49 ministers, 11 vice presidents and one crown prince, to attend High-Level Week, U.N. spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric told reporters Friday. Member states have submitted approximately 1,000 requests for bilateral meetings, while about 168 events are scheduled alongside the official proceedings. The 81st General Assembly's General Debate begins Tuesday and runs through Sept. 28. Beyond Iran, world leaders are expected to address Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the future of Gaza, international security and the U.N.'s ability to respond to emerging global challenges. Waltz described the administration's approach with a slogan inspired by the president's political branding: "Make the U.N. great again." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But the immediate diplomatic questions facing Washington are more concrete: whether allies will increase pressure on Iran, whether Gulf leaders can agree on a path toward ending the conflict and whether the administration's push for a leaner U.N. can coexist with its efforts to use the organization to address international security challenges.

articles.title: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King
articles.summary: Earl Spencer speaks to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the publication of his book about his sister Diana, Princess of Wales.
articles.body:
Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Charles, was his "duty...as an eyewitness to history".

In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the memoir's release on Tuesday, Earl Spencer said he wanted "to put things down once and for all that were true".

Among claims made in Swan Song about the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, was that he said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Here are the key moments from Earl Spencer's interview, which include his first account of how he was told about Diana's death and criticism of press coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

Earl initially told Diana's crash was 'not too serious'

Earl Spencer was in South Africa when Princess Diana died in a Paris car crash in the early hours of 31 August 1997, along with close friend Dodi Fayed and the driver of the car.

He told the BBC he got a call in the middle of the night from his sister Lady Jane Fellowes, who said Princess Diana had been in a crash but "it's not too serious".

But then he "kept getting more and more distressing calls" from his sister.

"And then my sister Jane said, 'I'm afraid she's died.' It started... as a little prang, and then it became a broken leg, perhaps a head injury, and then death."

Charles had 'giddy tone' after Diana's death

Describing the hours after her death, Earl Spencer said he took a call at his home in Cape Town from Prince Charles, who told him how he broke the news to Princes William and Harry at Balmoral Castle.

"I felt there was a sort of giddy tone," he told the BBC.

"I'd had a lot of calls that day from people who cared, who were stunned... and I just felt there was a lightness in his tone about Diana's death that really jarred with me."

In his book, Earl Spencer compares his tone to like a "lottery winner" and says he suspects the prince's reaction was based on how this event would free him to marry the woman he loved, his future wife Queen Camilla.

When asked by Kuenssberg if he could be sure that is what Prince Charles was thinking, Earl Spencer said: "I cannot be sure, I'm saying that's what I assume from the tone is a possibility."

Comments 'will not be a surprise' to William and Harry

Earl Spencer told the BBC he had been discussing funeral arrangements with a palace official, who said it had been agreed Princes William and Harry should walk behind their mother's coffin. Unhappy, he said he told the official it is not what his sister would have wanted, before the conversation came to an end.

Soon after, the earl says he took a call from Prince Charles, who asked him about his opposition to it.

"I said, 'Well, of course not, sir, she wouldn't want it'. And then he said, 'Well, I walked behind Lord Mountbatten's coffin.' And I said, 'Yes, but you were 30 and he wasn't your mother'."

He then claims Charles went "ballistic... and ranted for a while" about the Spencer's sense of duty not being adequate enough before "he said 'We'll forget her [Diana] soon enough'."

"I really was so stunned and after a stunned silence I said 'I can not believe you just said that' and I hung up on him", the earl told Kuenssberg during his sit down interview at his Althorp estate.

Responding to the Palace's statement pushing back on the story, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said.

"I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage in my life.

"I was hyper-alert to what he was saying, and those are precisely the words he said. And I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said.

"I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

The earl said he told "close friends and family" about the "monstrous" comment.

When asked if people should believe him or the King, he said: "Well, I'm telling the truth... what else would have made me hang up on the King that day?"

On what Princes William and Harry might think of the comments being brought up nearly 30 years later, he added the words "will not be a surprise" to the brothers.

He also said his renowned funeral eulogy , in which he said his sister's qualities would never be "extinguished from our minds", was a "direct rebuttal" of the prince's comments.

'I know lots of things about the King' not in the book

Talking about his motivations for writing the book, Earl Spencer, aged 62, said it was his "duty... as an eyewitness to history" and as someone in the "final season of my life" with his parents dying in their sixties.

"I'm aware of mortality and I wanted to just put things down once and for all that were true," the historian and journalist explained.

"This is not a threat, it's a fact, I know lots of things about the King which I chose not to include in the book because they were not relevant."

When put to him that the statement sounded like a threat when it involved potentially damaging information, he said: "No, not at all a threat, it's just the reality."

Kuenssberg questioned why he included an account of a conversation in which his sister told him Prince Charles was in love with his valet - a claim Earl Spencer said was improbable - and asked if he was motivated in including some of these allegations to create interest to sell the book.

"It's in the context of a conversation where Diana is telling me that her marriage is over," the earl replied.

"It's a brother's tribute, a loving tribute to a sister. And I think she deserves honesty so that's what I've delivered."

Harry and Meghan's media treatment 'echoes' Diana

When asked about how he thinks Prince Harry has been treated by the Royal Family, Earl Spencer told the BBC he is reluctant to discuss it, but he said he was concerned about his security.

"I would say that I personally worry about the fifth-in-line to the throne who's served in the military not having any police protection," he said.

"As an uncle who's seen his sister die in very, very preventable circumstances, that I would veer towards protection."

It is understood the committee that oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now they and their two children are full-time residents in the UK rather than visitors.

When asked about how the press treated Princess Diana and now Prince Harry and Meghan, he said tabloid articles "could be really really unpleasant".

"It would really be beholden on people to learn from Diana's example. I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life," Earl Spencer said.

"[Diana] was really brought low by all that criticism. And yeah I suppose it's a pity when I see echoes of that now."

Earl Spencer said he did not take sides - as he perceives is the "perception in the media" - in the dispute between Princes William and Harry.

"I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them. And if either of them wanted anything then I'd be equally there for them," he said.

"And I never get involved in one camp or the other, except as a benign figure I hope."

He said there are a "lot of reasons on both sides" why the brothers' relationship had "got to this stage".

"I hope one day it's resolved, but I don't know all – I certainly don't know what's been done in the finer detail and so I would feel intrusive if I got more involved than to say of course a mother would want her two sons to be happy together and love each other," he said.

Diana 'convinced she couldn't trust people' after Bashir interview

Reflecting on the time before Princess Diana's death, Kuenssberg asked if the infamous BBC Panorama interview with journalist Martin Bashir in 1995 might have been linked indirectly to his sister finding herself in Paris in 1997.

Shortly after the interview broadcast, in which Princess Diana admitted having an affair and said Prince Charles's affair with then-Camilla Parker Bowles made her feel worthless, the Queen wrote to Prince Charles and Princess Diana telling them to divorce.

A 2021 inquiry found Bashir acted in a "deceitful" way by mocking up fake bank statements - which falsely suggested individuals were being paid to keep Diana under surveillance - and showing them to Earl Spencer to gain access to the late princess.

Earl Spencer said he did make "a connection" between the crash and the Panorama interview and said they conned both him and Diana.

"People said, 'Oh, she was paranoid'. She wasn't paranoid. She was convinced that she couldn't trust people because the evidence was there. And, you know, I think that left her vulnerable that night."

The BBC and Bashir apologised to King Charles, Earl Spencer and Princes William and Harry after the 2021 report was published.

The BBC's then-director general, Tim Davie, said: "Although the report states that Diana, Princess of Wales, was keen on the idea of an interview with the BBC, it is clear that the process for securing the interview fell far short of what audiences have a right to expect. We are very sorry for this."

Earl Spencer, the ninth earl of an aristocratic family whose peerage dates back to the 18th Century and retains its vast estate, told the BBC he is "all for a monarchy, but I like a modern monarchy".

Talking about the "jarring" protocol around the monarchy, he said: "You know, you mentioned the statement earlier, 'His Majesty says", I just don't think it's healthy for a human being to be seen in such archaic, servile terms."

When Kuenssberg asked him if he supported this monarchy, following the damning book he has just written, he said: "I do."

He added when challenged: "Well, I'm not dealing with King Charles as monarch in this book, this is all 30-odd years ago and what was said and done then."

An emotional tribute to a sister he misses every day

As the interview came to an end, Earl Spencer was asked whether he would ever be able to get over his sister's death.

Visibly emotional, he said he misses Diana "every day", adding "that's the thing with sibling loss, you never get over it."

But his upcoming book, he said, is a way for him to have a final say on Diana's life before stepping off "into the sunset".

"One of the reasons I called this Swan Song actually is because it's my sign off," he said.

"I have been Diana's brother, this is my final take on the situation… I'm not here to bang on about Diana, this is my final word, a celebration of her."

articles.title: Gwynedd tourism tax plans delayed as thousands respond to consultation
articles.summary: The visitor levy would charge a nightly rate for people staying overnight in visitor accommodation.
articles.body:
A council looks set to delay its decision on imposing a tourism tax in Gwynedd after a public consultation prompted thousands of responses from visitors, residents and businesses.

A report to Cyngor Gwynedd said the number of responses - of which there were 6,856 - exceeded expectations.

This meant it had "not been possible to analyse, process and consider all the consultation responses" within an agreed deadline, it said.

The majority of businesses and visitors who responded said they were opposed to imposing the visitor levy, while 48.7% of residents supported it.

The council, which has to give 12 months' notice before imposing such a levy, had been aiming for October 2027.

The authority was due to present a report to councillors on Thursday and then give notice to the Welsh Revenue Authority (WRA) of any plan to introduce the levy.

The report said it had received "clear legal advice that it is not possible to proceed with a decision on the levy in September, 2026", as originally intended.

It said the response to the public consultation had been "significant" compared with the numbers received by neighbouring councils for Anglesey (2,000), and Conwy (1,300).

48.7% of Gwynedd residents supported the visitor levy with 43.5% opposing it

14.7% of businesses supported it, while 79.5% had opposed

10.7% of visitors supported, with 79.9% opposed

22.7% combined visitors, residents and businesses supported it, and 68.5% opposed

The visitor levy, or tourism tax, would charge a nightly rate for people staying overnight in visitor accommodation, such as hotels, B&Bs, self-catering accommodation, holiday caravans, campsites, hostels and shared accommodation, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

Fees for hostels, shared rooms and tent pitches would be 75p + VAT (£0.90) per person per night, while most other types of accommodation would be charged at £1.30 + VAT (£1.56).

Exceptions would include visitors under the age of 18 and those staying in tent pitches or shared accommodation, and where a stay lasts more than 31 nights within a single booking or where accommodation is emergency or temporary housing arranged by a local authority.

Considering the consultation extension of 11 days from 20 May to 26 July, the high number of responses, and the range of issues raised, the report to this Thursday's full council meeting stated it was "not currently in a position to make a decision".

It also pointed out the consultation was not about "whether respondents were 'for' or 'against'" the levy.

"Rather, it was a consultation to identify the potential impacts of introducing a visitor levy in the county and to assist in reaching a decision," it added.

articles.title: BJP, Congress trade barbs over PM Modi mimicry at Rahul Gandhi’s Indore event
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: BJP on Sunday criticised the Congress after stand-up comedian Pulkit Mani mimicked Prime Minister Narendra Modi during an event attended by.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP on Sunday criticised the Congress after stand-up comedian Pulkit Mani mimicked Prime Minister Narendra Modi during an event attended by party leader Rahul Gandhi in Madhya Pradesh, with Union ministers and other BJP leaders targeting the opposition party and Congress MP over the performance.The comedian performed the skit with the Rae Bareli MP during the latest edition of the ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event in Indore on Saturday. A video of the performance was shared by the Congress on X.In the short act, Mani came on stage laughing and hugged Rahul. “My friend. How are you?” he said. The Congress leader replied, “I'm fine; how are you, Modi ji?” Mani responded, “Great harassment”, and continued laughing while repeatedly using the phrase “my friend”.Rahul then said, “Very nice to meet you,” and asked Mani to “tell me more”. The comedian continued laughing and hugging Gandhi before saying, “Maa ko kursi do, maa”, while pointing towards the audience.BJP leaders hit out at Rahul GandhiUnion minister Piyush Goyal reacted to the performance on X, calling Rahul “Asanskari naraz fufa (uncultured disgruntled uncle).”“The irony writes itself. The need to come on stage every now and then just to drag Prime Minister Modi ji's name into cheap political theatre never fails to amaze me,” Goyal said, asking the former Congress president to “look in the mirror”.Union minister Kiren Rijiju also criticised Rahul, saying, “I hadn't imagined that a party which was in power for nearly six decades would turn into such a circus that is busy entertaining their own shrunken supporters.”Rijiju said Indians were proud that Prime Minister Modi was the “most popular” elected leader in the world.“Congress party has become a party of comedians and Jokers! They are out forever.... RIP,” he said.“Do you feel absolutely no shame in mocking an elderly mother and the Prime Minister of India?” Rijiju asked Rahul, while posting a video of PM Modi in which the prime minister is seen asking for a chair for an elderly woman who had attended one of his programmes.BJP national general secretary Smriti Irani also reacted to the controversy, writing in Hindi on X, “Jab nash manuj per chata hai, pehle vivek mar jaata hai” (When doom looms over a person, it's his conscience that dies first).BJP national secretary Sandeep Pathak called the mimicry act an expression of “desperation” and the “growing intellectual bankruptcy” of the Congress.“When you lose touch with India's values, you lose touch with India itself. And that is precisely where the Congress has lost its way,” Pathak, a Rajya Sabha MP, said on X.Congress leaders defend programmeCongress leader Bhupesh Baghel hit back at the BJP's criticism, saying every person's mother deserved respect and questioning why similar concerns were not raised when the mothers of Rahul and other leaders were allegedly insulted.“Everyone's mother is a mother, not PM Modi's mother alone. Why are their feelings not hurt when they insult Rahul Gandhi's mother or other leaders' mothers? This culture of insulting mothers was started by BJP-RSS and Mahamanav,” Baghel said.Congress MP Imraan Masood said the ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ programme had “shattered eardrums” of BJP leaders.“Let the elections come. They will find out soon enough. 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' has shattered their eardrums. They see Rahul Gandhi in their dreams and wake up with a start,” Masood said in Ranchi.Congress leader TS Singh Deo said criticism and mimicry should not be objected to, but opposed the use of abusive language in public conversations.“I do not think it is acceptable to stoop to the level of abusive language in a public conversation. But beyond that, if you're criticising someone in a normal way, even in a joking manner or with mimicry, no one should have any objection to it,” he said in Raipur.AICC general secretary Ghulam Ahmad Mir said the programme had received an overwhelming response and claimed that more than 200,000 young people had attended events under the initiative across India and Madhya Pradesh.Rahul Gandhi had addressed students at the Indore session on issues including education costs and employment opportunities.Congress leaders said the programme was focused on issues faced by young people and student welfare.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
